meta.title: Who really said "Spare the rod and spoil the child"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: It isn't in the Bible. The exact proverb was coined by Samuel Butler in his 1663 satire Hudibras — as a dirty joke, not a parenting rule.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Spare the rod and spoil the child'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Scripture. The phrase was coined by Samuel Butler in Hudibras (1663) — a bawdy joke, later mistaken for the Bible's Proverbs 13:24.

answer.label: Not the Bible — coined by Samuel Butler
answer.sourceLine: The exact proverb appears in no Bible translation. Its earliest documented form is in Butler’s mock-heroic poem “Hudibras” (Part II, Canto I; registered 5 Nov 1663, printed 1664), where a widow deploys it as a bawdy joke. Scripture inspired the idea — Proverbs 13:24 — but never carried this wording.

source.heading: Where the phrase actually comes from
source.excerpt:
What medicine else can cure the fits
Of lovers when they lose their wits?
Love is a boy by poets stil’d;
Then spare the rod, and spoil the child.
trail: The exact phrase is absent from Scripture; per Wikipedia, it originates in Samuel Butler’s “Hudibras.”
Word Histories dates the earliest attestation to “Hudibras: the second part” (London, 1664) and gives Proverbs 13:24 as the KJV source of the sentiment.
This Day in Quotes quotes the full couplet and notes Part II was entered in the Stationers’ Register on 5 Nov 1663 in a bawdy, satirical context.
source.cutTag: the rhyming couplet Butler made famous
source.excerptNote: The lines are a widow’s ribald tease, not a parenting maxim — Butler was mocking, not moralising. Proverbs 13:24 (KJV, 1611) reads instead: “He that spareth his rod hateth his son: but he that loveth him chasteneth him betimes.”
source.rightsNote: Butler’s “Hudibras, Part II” was first published in 1664, and the King James Bible in 1611 — both are long in the public domain in the United States.

author.heading: About Samuel Butler
author.bio: Samuel Butler (1613–1680) was an English poet best known for Hudibras, a mock-heroic satire ridiculing the Puritans and religious hypocrisy of his day. Published in three parts (1663, 1664, 1678), the poem was hugely popular at the Restoration court and coined several phrases that outlived their bawdy origins — including “spare the rod and spoil the child.”

misattribution.heading: Why people think it’s in the Bible
misattribution.intro: The line sounds scriptural and echoes a real proverb, so it is routinely quoted as the word of God. It isn’t.

items.why: No Bible version — KJV, NIV, or otherwise — contains the phrase “spare the rod and spoil the child.” The nearest verse, Proverbs 13:24, reads “He that spareth his rod hateth his son.”
In Hudibras the words are a widow’s ribald tease about love and whipping, not advice on raising children — a satirical inversion, not a moral maxim.

misattribution.truthLine: The sentiment is biblical, but the exact wording was coined by Samuel Butler in 1663–64.

context.heading: Idea vs. wording
lead: The confusion is understandable: the Book of Proverbs really does link the “rod” to discipline in several verses, and English speakers absorbed that idea for centuries. Butler simply gave it a catchy, rhyming, alliterative shape — and did so as a joke, putting it in the mouth of a flirtatious widow.

Once the couplet caught on, the memorable Butler wording detached from its satirical setting and floated back toward the scripture that inspired it, until most people assumed they were quoting the Bible directly.
context.pull: The thought is Solomon’s; the sentence is Butler’s.
